I am not fully certain this rises to a hard error given it may be an intentional externalization pattern, so I mark this UNCERTAIN rather than MATERIAL.

findings.verifierReasoning: The source defines a bounded PERIOD with two independently operative components: (1) an entry test (PMV < 70% of Initial PMV) and (2) a distinct termination test (PMV becomes >= Initial PMV), plus an express carve-out that the period does NOT exist at all if it is actually (ignoring clause (ii) of the Second Deleveraging Trigger Period definition) a Second Deleveraging Trigger Period. findings.sourceCitation: §1.01 (definitions of "Deleveraging Trigger Period" and "Second Deleveraging Trigger Period")
findings.proposedIrEvidence: Each EVENT_ACTIVE node's actually-evaluable "triggerCondition" is a bare point-in-time COMPARE: Prevailing Market Value LT (0.7 * Initial Prevailing Market Value) for Deleveraging Trigger Period, or LT (0.5 * Initial Prevailing Market Value) for Second Deleveraging Trigger Period. The true exit/recovery threshold (100% of Initial, or hand-off to the milder period) is only captured as a free-text "activeDuration" string, not as part of any computable expression used elsewhere (e.g. Applicable Margin's IF.condition, or the LTV-table IFs, all reference only the entry-threshold triggerCondition).
findings.verifierReasoning: The source defines these as stateful, hysteretic periods: entry occurs at one threshold (70% or 50% of Initial Prevailing Market Value) but exit only occurs at a materially higher/different threshold (100% of Initial, or transition to the other trigger tier). The proposed IR's computable logic collapses this into a single stateless point-in-time comparison against only the entry threshold. Concretely: if collateral value falls to 60% of Initial (triggering Deleveraging Trigger Period at the 70% entry threshold) and later recovers to 85% of Initial, the source still treats the period as in effect (recovery requires >=100%), so the 4.75%/higher-LTV tier logic wired off of it (e.g., Applicable Margin, Liquidation/Top Up/Initial/Release LTV) should still apply; but the IR's triggerCondition (value < 70%*Initial) would evaluate to false at 85%, so any engine driven solely by the computable triggerCondition would incorrectly conclude the trigger period has ended and revert to the non-triggered margin/LTV tier. This changes the applicable interest rate and the LTV thresholds governing margin calls, forced liquidation, and collateral release - core economic terms. Notably, "Deleveraging Trigger Period" itself is honestly marked sufficiency PARTIAL (suggesting the compiler recognized this gap), yet "Second Deleveraging Trigger Period", "Applicable Margin", "Liquidation LTV", "Top Up LTV", "Initial LTV", and "Release LTV" - all of which embed the identical simplified entry-only trigger logic - are marked sufficiency COMPLETE. That inconsistency is itself evidence the COMPLETE markings are unreliable here.

findings.sourceEvidence: The Existing Credit Agreement shall be amended and restated in the form of this Agreement with effect from the first date on which the following conditions precedent are satisfied: ... (d) The Borrower shall have notified the Lender in writing as to the proposed Amendment and Restatement Effective Date.
findings.verifierReasoning: Section 3.03(d) is framed strictly as one of five enumerated conditions precedent (a)-(e) that gate whether and when the Existing Credit Agreement is amended and restated - the consequence of non-satisfaction is simply that the Amendment and Restatement Effective Date does not occur, not that the Borrower is in breach of a freestanding covenant. Labeling this as posture 'OBLIGATION' with action 'OTHER' could be read by a downstream compliance engine as an independently enforceable affirmative covenant of the Borrower (breach of which could trigger a Default), rather than as a mere condition-precedent prong to contractual effectiveness. I cannot fully rule out that the IR schema intends 'OBLIGATION' generically for any 'Borrower shall have done X' condition-precedent clause, so I flag this as uncertain rather than definitively wrong, but it is a plausible mischaracterization of legal effect worth scrutiny.

findings.sourceEvidence: (a) ...all notices and other communications provided for hereunder shall be delivered by hand or overnight courier service...; (c) The Lender or the Borrower may, in its discretion, agree to accept notices and other communications to it hereunder by electronic communications...; (e) Change of Address, etc. Any party hereto may change its address or facsimile number for notices and other communications hereunder by notice to the other parties hereto.
findings.proposedIrEvidence: Every rule derived from Section 7.02 (ir-rule:e43eb19fc85a7b35d68a75bc, d90d72ac2cebd7371f2b012c, e07cf4b873b69f4432b46861, 904d9e9cd0b0e8b8a325ae9f, 254d64bfa56370677730ada4, 66a3e66744df2b08af0686eb) sets entityScope to ['BORROWER'] only, with entityScopeExcluded empty.
findings.verifierReasoning: Section 7.02 is a mutual/bilateral notices article. The delivery-method obligation in (a) governs 'all notices and other communications provided for hereunder' regardless of which party is the sender - it plainly also binds the Lender, Collateral Agent, and Administrative Agent when they send notices (subclause (ii) even addresses where notices to the Lender/Collateral Agent/Administrative Agent go). Subsection (c)'s second sentence expressly gives the right to accept electronic notices to 'the Lender or the Borrower,' and subsection (e) expressly states 'any party hereto may change its address.' By scoping every rule to entityScope ['BORROWER'] only (with several also marked sufficiency COMPLETE), the proposed IR would mislead a reviewer into concluding these notice obligations/rights run only to or from the Borrower, when the source text is symmetric/multi-party. A concrete divergence: if the Lender sends a default notice by an unlisted method, or changes its own Lending Office address without following the (e) procedure, a reviewer relying on this IR (scoped only to Borrower) could wrongly conclude Section 7.02 does not govern that conduct at all, when the source text says it does.

findings.sourceEvidence: Notices and other communications to the Lender hereunder may be delivered or furnished by electronic communication...pursuant to procedures approved by the Lender, provided that the foregoing shall not apply to notices to the Lender pursuant to Article II if the Lender has notified the Borrower that it is incapable of receiving notices under such Article by electronic communication. The Lender or the Borrower may, in its discretion, agree to accept notices and other communications to it hereunder by electronic communications pursuant to procedures approved by it; provided that approval of such procedures may be limited to particular notices or communications.
findings.proposedIrEvidence: rule[r3].condition[1] models the second sentence ('The Lender or the Borrower may, in its discretion, agree to accept notices...pursuant to procedures approved by it...') as a 'condition' of the single permission rule ir-rule:904d9e9cd0b0e8b8a325ae9f, whose primary condition[0] and exception[0] are drawn from the first sentence (notices to the Lender under Lender-approved procedures, with the Article II carve-out).
findings.verifierReasoning: The two sentences of 7.02(c) grant two distinct, independently operative rights: the first is a specific permission for notices to the Lender under Lender-approved procedures (subject to the Article II carve-out); the second is a broader, separate, symmetric right for either the Lender or the Borrower to agree to accept electronic notices under its own approved procedures, which need not depend on satisfaction of the first sentence's terms. Modeling the second sentence as a 'condition' nested under a single permission rule keyed to the first sentence's carve-out risks implying the second right is gated by or subordinate to the first sentence's Article II exception, when the source presents them as independent, parallel grants. A reviewer could wrongly conclude the Borrower's or Lender's bilateral right to accept electronic notices under self-approved procedures is unavailable whenever the Article II carve-out in the first sentence is triggered, which the source does not actually say.
